<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

</span>
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>NVIDIA
</span>
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_email"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Email: </span><a href="mailto:"><span id="id5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">dally@stanford.edu</span></a>
</span></span></span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Deep neural networks are widely used in machine learning applications. However, the deployment of large neural networks models can be difficult to deploy on mobile devices with limited power budgets. To solve this problem, we propose Trained Ternary Quantization (TTQ), a method that can reduce the precision of weights in neural networks to ternary values. This method has very little accuracy degradation and can even improve the accuracy of some models (32, 44, 56-layer ResNet) on CIFAR-10 and AlexNet on ImageNet. And our AlexNet model is trained from scratch, which means it’s as easy as to train normal full precision model. We highlight our trained quantization method that can learn both ternary values and ternary assignment. During inference, only ternary values (2-bit weights) and scaling factors are needed, therefore our models are nearly <math id="abstract1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="16\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>16</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">16\times</annotation></semantics></math> smaller than full-precision models. Our ternary models can also be viewed as sparse binary weight networks, which can potentially be accelerated with custom circuit. Experiments on CIFAR-10 show that the ternary models obtained by trained quantization method <em id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">outperform</em> full-precision models of ResNet-32,44,56 by 0.04%, 0.16%, 0.36%, respectively. On ImageNet, our model outperforms full-precision AlexNet model by 0.3% of Top-1 accuracy and outperforms previous ternary models by 3%.</p>
  
</div>
<div id="p1" class="ltx_para">
<table id="p1.1" class="ltx_tabular ltx_align_top">
<tbody class="ltx_tbody">
<tr id="p1.1.1" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="p1.1.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left"><span class="ltx_rule" style="width:0.0pt;height:24.0pt;--ltx-bg-color:black;display:inline-block;"></span></td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Deep neural networks are becoming the preferred approach for many machine learning applications. However, as networks get deeper, deploying a network with a large number of parameters on a small device becomes increasingly difficult. Much work has been
done to reduce the size of networks. Half-precision networks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Amodei et al., 2015</a>)</cite> cut sizes of neural networks in half. XNOR-Net <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rastegari et al., 2016</a>)</cite>, DoReFa-Net <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2016</a>)</cite> and network binarization <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Courbariaux et al., </a>; <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Courbariaux et al., 2015</a>; <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lin et al., 2015</a>)</cite> use aggressively quantized weights, activations and gradients to further reduce computation during training. While weight binarization benefits from <math id="S1.p1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="32\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>32</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">32\times</annotation></semantics></math> smaller model size, the extreme compression rate comes with a loss of accuracy. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hubara et al. (2016)</a></cite> and <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li &amp; Liu (2016)</a></cite> propose ternary weight networks to trade off between model size and accuracy.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In this paper, we propose Trained Ternary Quantization which uses two full-precision scaling coefficients <math id="S1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W^{p}_{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>W</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>p</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W^{p}_{l}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W^{n}_{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>W</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>n</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W^{n}_{l}</annotation></semantics></math> for each layer <math id="S1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="l" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>l</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">l</annotation></semantics></math>, and quantize the weights to {<math id="S1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-W^{n}_{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>−</mo><msubsup><mi>W</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>n</mi></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-W^{n}_{l}</annotation></semantics></math>, 0, <math id="S1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="+W^{p}_{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>+</mo><msubsup><mi>W</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>p</mi></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+W^{p}_{l}</annotation></semantics></math>} instead of traditional {-1, 0, +1} or {-E, 0, +E} where E is the mean of the absolute weight value, which is not learned. Our positive and negative weights have different absolute values <math id="S1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W^{p}_{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>W</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>p</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W^{p}_{l}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S1.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W^{n}_{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>W</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>n</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W^{n}_{l}</annotation></semantics></math> that are trainable parameters. We also maintain latent full-precision weights at training time, and discard them at test time. We back propagate the gradient to both <math id="S1.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W^{p}_{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>W</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>p</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W^{p}_{l}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S1.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W^{n}_{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>W</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>n</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W^{n}_{l}</annotation></semantics></math> and to the latent full-precision weights. This makes it possible to adjust the ternary assignment (i.e. which of the three values a weight is assigned).</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Our quantization method, achieves higher accuracy on the CIFAR-10 and ImageNet datasets. For AlexNet on ImageNet dataset, our method outperforms previously state-of-art ternary network<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li &amp; Liu, 2016</a>)</cite> by 3.0% of Top-1 accuracy and the full-precision model by 1.6%. By converting most of the parameters to 2-bit values, we also compress the network by about 16x. Moreover, the advantage of few multiplications still remains, because <math id="S1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W^{p}_{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>W</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>p</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W^{p}_{l}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W^{n}_{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>W</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>n</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W^{n}_{l}</annotation></semantics></math> are fixed for each layer during inference. On custom hardware, multiplications can be pre-computed on activations, so only two multiplications per activation are required.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Motivations</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The potential of deep neural networks, once deployed to mobile devices, has the advantage of lower latency, no reliance on the network, and better user privacy. However, energy efficiency becomes the bottleneck for deploying deep neural networks on mobile devices because mobile devices are battery constrained. Current deep neural network models consist of hundreds of millions of parameters. Reducing the size of a DNN model makes the deployment on edge devices easier.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">First, a smaller model means less overhead when exporting models to clients. Take autonomous driving for example; Tesla periodically copies new models from their servers to customers’ cars. Smaller models require less communication in such over-the-air updates, making frequent updates more feasible. Another example is on Apple Store; apps above 100 MB will not download until you connect to Wi-Fi. It’s infeasible to put a large DNN model in an app. The second issue is energy consumption. Deep learning is energy consuming, which is problematic for battery-constrained mobile devices. As a result, iOS 10 requires iPhone to be plugged with charger while performing photo analysis. Fetching DNN models from memory takes more than two orders of magnitude more energy than arithmetic operations. Smaller neural networks require less memory bandwidth to fetch the model, saving the energy and extending battery life. The third issue is area cost. When deploying DNNs on Application-Specific Integrated Circuits (ASICs), a sufficiently small model can be stored directly on-chip, and smaller models enable a smaller ASIC die.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Several previous works aimed to improve energy and spatial efficiency of deep networks. One common strategy proven useful is to quantize 32-bit weights to one or two bits, which greatly reduces model size and saves memory reference. However, experimental results show that compressed weights usually come with degraded performance, which is a great loss for some performance-sensitive applications. The contradiction between compression and performance motivates us to work on trained ternary quantization, minimizing performance degradation of deep neural networks while saving as much energy and space as possible.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Related Work</h2>

<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Binary Neural Network (BNN)</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lin et al. (2015)</a></cite> proposed binary and ternary connections to compress neural networks and speed up computation during inference. They used similar probabilistic methods to convert 32-bit weights into binary values or ternary values, defined as:</p>
<table id="S3.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\begin{split}w^{b}\sim{\rm Bernoulli}(\frac{\tilde{w}+1}{2})\times{2}-1\\
w^{t}\sim{\rm Bernoulli}(|\tilde{w}|)\times{\text{sign}(\tilde{w})}\end{split}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mtable displaystyle="true" rowspacing="0pt"><mtr><mtd class="ltx_align_right" columnalign="right"><mrow><msup><mi>w</mi><mi>b</mi></msup><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>Bernoulli</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>w</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd class="ltx_align_right" columnalign="right"><mrow><msup><mi>w</mi><mi>t</mi></msup><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>Bernoulli</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>w</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mtext>sign</mtext></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>w</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\begin{split}w^{b}\sim{\rm Bernoulli}(\frac{\tilde{w}+1}{2})\times{2}-1\\
w^{t}\sim{\rm Bernoulli}(|\tilde{w}|)\times{\text{sign}(\tilde{w})}\end{split}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">Here <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w^{b}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>w</mi><mi>b</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w^{b}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w^{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>w</mi><mi>t</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w^{t}</annotation></semantics></math> denote binary and ternary weights after quantization. <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{w}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>w</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{w}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the latent full precision weight.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">During back-propagation, as the above quantization equations are not differentiable, derivatives of expectations of the Bernoulli distribution are computed instead, yielding the identity function:</p>
<table id="S3.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{\partial L}{\partial\tilde{w}}=\frac{\partial L}{\partial w^{b}}=\frac{\partial L}{\partial w^{t}}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>w</mi><mo>~</mo></mover></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>∂</mo><msup><mi>w</mi><mi>b</mi></msup></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>∂</mo><msup><mi>w</mi><mi>t</mi></msup></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{\partial L}{\partial\tilde{w}}=\frac{\partial L}{\partial w^{b}}=\frac{\partial L}{\partial w^{t}}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.2" class="ltx_p">Here <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>L</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L</annotation></semantics></math> is the loss to optimize.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">For BNN with binary connections, only quantized binary values are needed for inference. Therefore a <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="32\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>32</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">32\times</annotation></semantics></math> smaller model can be deployed into applications.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>DoReFa-Net</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al. (2016)</a></cite> proposed DoReFa-Net which quantizes weights, activations and gradients of neural networks using different widths of bits. Therefore with specifically designed low-bit multiplication algorithm or hardware, both training and inference stages can be accelerated.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">They also introduced a much simpler method to quantize 32-bit weights to binary values, defined as:</p>
<table id="S3.E3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w^{b}=\boldsymbol{E}(|\tilde{w}|)\times\text{sign}(\tilde{w})" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>w</mi><mi>b</mi></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>𝑬</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>w</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mtext>sign</mtext></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>w</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w^{b}=\boldsymbol{E}(|\tilde{w}|)\times\text{sign}(\tilde{w})</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(3)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.2" class="ltx_p">Here <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\boldsymbol{E}(|\tilde{w}|)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝑬</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>w</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\boldsymbol{E}(|\tilde{w}|)</annotation></semantics></math> calculates the mean of absolute values of full precision weights <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{w}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>w</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{w}</annotation></semantics></math> as layer-wise scaling factors. During back-propagation, Equation <a href="#S3.E2" title="In 3.1 Binary Neural Network (BNN) ‣ 3 Related Work ‣ Trained Ternary Quantization" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> still applies.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3 </span>Ternary Weight Networks</h3>

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li &amp; Liu (2016)</a></cite> proposed TWN (Ternary weight networks), which reduce accuracy loss of binary networks by introducing zero as a third quantized value. They use two symmetric thresholds <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pm\Delta_{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>±</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pm\Delta_{l}</annotation></semantics></math> and a scaling factor <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{l}</annotation></semantics></math> for each layer <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="l" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>l</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">l</annotation></semantics></math> to quantize weighs into <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{-W_{l},0,+W_{l}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></mrow><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{-W_{l},0,+W_{l}\}</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>
<table id="S3.E4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E4.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="w^{t}_{l}=\left\{\begin{aligned} W_{l}&amp;:\tilde{w}_{l}&gt;\Delta_{l}\\
0&amp;:|\tilde{w}_{l}|\leq\Delta_{l}\\
-W_{l}&amp;:\tilde{w}_{l}&lt;-\Delta_{l}\end{aligned}\right." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>w</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>t</mi></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>{</mo><mtable columnspacing="0pt" displaystyle="true" rowspacing="0pt"><mtr><mtd class="ltx_align_right" columnalign="right"><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></mtd><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>w</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>&gt;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></mrow></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd class="ltx_align_right" columnalign="right"><mn>0</mn></mtd><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>w</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>l</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo>≤</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></mrow></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd class="ltx_align_right" columnalign="right"><mrow><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></mrow></mtd><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>w</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>&lt;</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w^{t}_{l}=\left\{\begin{aligned} W_{l}&amp;:\tilde{w}_{l}&gt;\Delta_{l}\\
0&amp;:|\tilde{w}_{l}|\leq\Delta_{l}\\
-W_{l}&amp;:\tilde{w}_{l}&lt;-\Delta_{l}\end{aligned}\right.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.2" class="ltx_p">They then solve an optimization problem of minimizing L2 distance between full precision and ternary weights to obtain layer-wise values of <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{l}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta_{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta_{l}</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>
<table id="S3.E5" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\begin{split}\Delta_{l}&amp;=0.7\times\boldsymbol{E}(|\tilde{w}_{l}|)\\
W_{l}&amp;=\underset{i\in\{i|\tilde{w}_{l}(i)|&gt;\Delta\}}{\boldsymbol{E}}(|\tilde{w}_{l}(i)|)\end{split}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mtable columnspacing="0pt" displaystyle="true" rowspacing="0pt"><mtr><mtd class="ltx_align_right" columnalign="right"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></mtd><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>0.7</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mrow><mi>𝑬</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>w</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>l</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd class="ltx_align_right" columnalign="right"><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></mtd><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><munder accentunder="true"><mi>𝑬</mi><mrow><mi mathsize="0.700em">i</mi><mo mathsize="0.700em">∈</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi mathsize="0.700em">i</mi><mo fence="false" maxsize="0.700em" minsize="0.700em" rspace="0.167em" stretchy="true">|</mo><mover accent="true"><mi mathsize="0.700em">w</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><msub><mrow></mrow><mi mathsize="0.710em">l</mi></msub><mo maxsize="0.700em" minsize="0.700em">(</mo><mi mathsize="0.700em">i</mi><mo maxsize="0.700em" minsize="0.700em">)</mo><mo fence="false" maxsize="0.700em" minsize="0.700em" stretchy="true">|</mo><mo lspace="0.167em" mathsize="0.700em">&gt;</mo><mi mathsize="0.700em" mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></munder><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>w</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>l</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\begin{split}\Delta_{l}&amp;=0.7\times\boldsymbol{E}(|\tilde{w}_{l}|)\\
W_{l}&amp;=\underset{i\in\{i|\tilde{w}_{l}(i)|&gt;\Delta\}}{\boldsymbol{E}}(|\tilde{w}_{l}(i)|)\end{split}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(5)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.3" class="ltx_p">And again Equation <a href="#S3.E2" title="In 3.1 Binary Neural Network (BNN) ‣ 3 Related Work ‣ Trained Ternary Quantization" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> is used to calculate gradients.
While an additional bit is required for ternary weights, TWN achieves a validation accuracy that is very close to full precision networks according to their paper.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.4 </span>Deep Compression</h3>

<div id="S3.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Han et al. (2015)</a></cite> proposed deep compression to prune away trivial connections and reduce precision of weights.
Unlike above models using zero or symmetric thresholds to quantize high precision weights, Deep Compression used clusters to categorize weights into groups. In Deep Compression, low precision weights are fine-tuned from a pre-trained full precision network, and the assignment of each weight is established at the beginning and stay unchanged, while representative value of each cluster is updated throughout fine-tuning.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Method</h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our method is illustrated in Figure <a href="#S4.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 4.1 Learning both Ternary Values and Ternary Assignments ‣ 4 Method ‣ Trained Ternary Quantization" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>. First, we normalize the full-precision weights to the range [-1, +1] by dividing each weight by the maximum weight. Next, we quantize the intermediate full-resolution weights to {-1, 0, +1} by thresholding. The threshold factor <math id="S4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> is a hyper-parameter that is the same across all the layers in order to reduce the search space. Finally, we perform trained quantization by back propagating two gradients, as shown in the dashed lines in Figure <a href="#S4.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 4.1 Learning both Ternary Values and Ternary Assignments ‣ 4 Method ‣ Trained Ternary Quantization" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>. We back-propagate <math id="S4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="gradient_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">gradient_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> to the full-resolution weights and <math id="S4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="gradient_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">gradient_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> to the scaling coefficients. The former enables learning the ternary <span id="S4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">assignments</span>, and the latter enables learning the ternary <span id="S4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">values</span>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">At inference time, we throw away the full-resolution weights and only use ternary weights.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Learning both Ternary Values and Ternary Assignments</h3>

<figure id="S4.F1" class="ltx_figure"><img src="1612.01064v3/process.png" id="S4.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:559/121;" width="559" height="121" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 1: </span>Overview of the trained ternary quantization procedure.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">During gradient descent we learn both the quantized ternary weights (the codebook), and choose which of these values is assigned to each weight (choosing the codebook index).</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To learn the ternary value (codebook), we introduce two quantization factors <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W^{p}_{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>W</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>p</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W^{p}_{l}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W^{n}_{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>W</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>n</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W^{n}_{l}</annotation></semantics></math> for positive and negative weights in each layer <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="l" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>l</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">l</annotation></semantics></math>. During feed-forward, quantized ternary weights <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w^{t}_{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>w</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>t</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w^{t}_{l}</annotation></semantics></math> are calculated as:</p>
<table id="S4.E6" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E6.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="w^{t}_{l}=\left\{\begin{aligned} W^{p}_{l}&amp;:\tilde{w}_{l}&gt;\Delta_{l}\\
0&amp;:|\tilde{w}_{l}|\leq\Delta_{l}\\
-W^{n}_{l}&amp;:\tilde{w}_{l}&lt;-\Delta_{l}\end{aligned}\right." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>w</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>t</mi></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>{</mo><mtable columnspacing="0pt" displaystyle="true" rowspacing="0pt"><mtr><mtd class="ltx_align_right" columnalign="right"><msubsup><mi>W</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>p</mi></msubsup></mtd><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>w</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>&gt;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></mrow></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd class="ltx_align_right" columnalign="right"><mn>0</mn></mtd><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>w</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>l</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo>≤</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></mrow></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd class="ltx_align_right" columnalign="right"><mrow><mo>−</mo><msubsup><mi>W</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>n</mi></msubsup></mrow></mtd><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>w</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>&lt;</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w^{t}_{l}=\left\{\begin{aligned} W^{p}_{l}&amp;:\tilde{w}_{l}&gt;\Delta_{l}\\
0&amp;:|\tilde{w}_{l}|\leq\Delta_{l}\\
-W^{n}_{l}&amp;:\tilde{w}_{l}&lt;-\Delta_{l}\end{aligned}\right.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(6)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Unlike previous work where quantized weights are calculated from 32-bit weights, the scaling coefficients <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W^{p}_{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>W</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>p</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W^{p}_{l}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W^{n}_{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>W</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>n</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W^{n}_{l}</annotation></semantics></math> are two independent parameters and are trained together with other parameters. Following the rule of gradient descent, derivatives of <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W^{p}_{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>W</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>p</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W^{p}_{l}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W^{n}_{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>W</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>n</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W^{n}_{l}</annotation></semantics></math> are calculated as:</p>
<table id="S4.E7" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{\partial L}{\partial W^{p}_{l}}=\sum_{i\in I^{p}_{l}}\frac{\partial L}{\partial w^{t}_{l}(i)},\frac{\partial L}{\partial W^{n}_{l}}=\sum_{i\in I^{n}_{l}}\frac{\partial L}{\partial w^{t}_{l}(i)}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>∂</mo><msubsup><mi>W</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>p</mi></msubsup></mrow></mfrac><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>∈</mo><msubsup><mi>I</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>p</mi></msubsup></mrow></munder><mfrac><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>w</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>t</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>∂</mo><msubsup><mi>W</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>n</mi></msubsup></mrow></mfrac><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>∈</mo><msubsup><mi>I</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>n</mi></msubsup></mrow></munder><mfrac><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>w</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>t</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{\partial L}{\partial W^{p}_{l}}=\sum_{i\in I^{p}_{l}}\frac{\partial L}{\partial w^{t}_{l}(i)},\frac{\partial L}{\partial W^{n}_{l}}=\sum_{i\in I^{n}_{l}}\frac{\partial L}{\partial w^{t}_{l}(i)}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(7)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS1.p3.2" class="ltx_p">Here <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I^{p}_{l}=\{i|\tilde{w}_{l}(i)&gt;\Delta_{l}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>I</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>p</mi></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>w</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>l</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>&gt;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I^{p}_{l}=\{i|\tilde{w}_{l}(i)&gt;\Delta_{l}\}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I^{n}_{l}=\{i|(i)\tilde{w}_{l}&lt;-\Delta_{l}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>I</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>n</mi></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>w</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>l</mi></msub></mrow><mo>&lt;</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I^{n}_{l}=\{i|(i)\tilde{w}_{l}&lt;-\Delta_{l}\}</annotation></semantics></math>. Furthermore, because of the existence of two scaling factors, gradients of latent full precision weights can no longer be calculated by Equation <a href="#S3.E2" title="In 3.1 Binary Neural Network (BNN) ‣ 3 Related Work ‣ Trained Ternary Quantization" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>. We use scaled gradients for 32-bit weights:</p>
<table id="S4.E8" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E8.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\frac{\partial L}{\partial\tilde{w}_{l}}=\left\{\begin{aligned} W^{p}_{l}\times\frac{\partial L}{\partial w^{t}_{l}}&amp;:\tilde{w}_{l}&gt;\Delta_{l}\\
1\times\frac{\partial L}{\partial w^{t}_{l}}&amp;:|\tilde{w}_{l}|\leq\Delta_{l}\\
W^{n}_{l}\times\frac{\partial L}{\partial w^{t}_{l}}&amp;:\tilde{w}_{l}&lt;-\Delta_{l}\end{aligned}\right." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>∂</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>w</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>l</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>{</mo><mtable columnspacing="0pt" displaystyle="true" rowspacing="0pt"><mtr><mtd class="ltx_align_right" columnalign="right"><mrow><msubsup><mi>W</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>p</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>∂</mo><msubsup><mi>w</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>t</mi></msubsup></mrow></mfrac></mrow></mtd><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>w</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>&gt;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></mrow></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd class="ltx_align_right" columnalign="right"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>∂</mo><msubsup><mi>w</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>t</mi></msubsup></mrow></mfrac></mrow></mtd><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>w</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>l</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo>≤</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></mrow></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd class="ltx_align_right" columnalign="right"><mrow><msubsup><mi>W</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>n</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>∂</mo><msubsup><mi>w</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>t</mi></msubsup></mrow></mfrac></mrow></mtd><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>w</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>&lt;</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{\partial L}{\partial\tilde{w}_{l}}=\left\{\begin{aligned} W^{p}_{l}\times\frac{\partial L}{\partial w^{t}_{l}}&amp;:\tilde{w}_{l}&gt;\Delta_{l}\\
1\times\frac{\partial L}{\partial w^{t}_{l}}&amp;:|\tilde{w}_{l}|\leq\Delta_{l}\\
W^{n}_{l}\times\frac{\partial L}{\partial w^{t}_{l}}&amp;:\tilde{w}_{l}&lt;-\Delta_{l}\end{aligned}\right.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(8)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Note we use scalar number 1 as factor of gradients of zero weights. The overall quantization process is illustrated as Figure <a href="#S4.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 4.1 Learning both Ternary Values and Ternary Assignments ‣ 4 Method ‣ Trained Ternary Quantization" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>. The evolution of the ternary weights from different layers during training is shown in Figure <a href="#S4.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 4.2 Quantization Heuristic ‣ 4 Method ‣ Trained Ternary Quantization" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>. We observe that as training proceeds, different layers behave differently: for the first quantized conv layer, the absolute values of <math id="S4.SS1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W^{p}_{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>W</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>p</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W^{p}_{l}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS1.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W^{n}_{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>W</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>n</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W^{n}_{l}</annotation></semantics></math> get smaller and sparsity gets lower, while for the last conv layer and fully connected layer, the absolute values of <math id="S4.SS1.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W^{p}_{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>W</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>p</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W^{p}_{l}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS1.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W^{n}_{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>W</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>n</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W^{n}_{l}</annotation></semantics></math> get larger and sparsity gets higher.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">We learn the ternary assignments (index to the codebook) by updating the latent full-resolution weights during training. This may cause the assignments to change between iterations. Note that the thresholds are not constants as the maximal absolute values change over time. Once an updated weight crosses the threshold, the ternary assignment is changed.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">The benefits of using trained quantization factors are: i) The asymmetry of <math id="S4.SS1.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W^{p}_{l}\neq W^{n}_{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>W</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>p</mi></msubsup><mo>≠</mo><msubsup><mi>W</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>n</mi></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W^{p}_{l}\neq W^{n}_{l}</annotation></semantics></math> enables neural networks to have more model capacity. ii) Quantized weights play the role of "learning rate multipliers" during back propagation.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Quantization Heuristic</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In previous work on ternary weight networks, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li &amp; Liu (2016)</a></cite> proposed Ternary Weight Networks (TWN) using <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pm\Delta_{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>±</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pm\Delta_{l}</annotation></semantics></math> as thresholds to reduce 32-bit weights to ternary values, where <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pm\Delta_{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>±</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pm\Delta_{l}</annotation></semantics></math> is defined as Equation <a href="#S3.E5" title="In 3.3 Ternary Weight Networks ‣ 3 Related Work ‣ Trained Ternary Quantization" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>. They optimized value of <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pm\Delta_{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>±</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pm\Delta_{l}</annotation></semantics></math> by minimizing expectation of L2 distance between full precision weights and ternary weights.
Instead of using a strictly optimized threshold, we adopt different heuristics: 1) use the maximum absolute value of the weights as a reference to the layer’s threshold and maintain a constant factor <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> for all layers:</p>
<table id="S4.E9" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta_{l}=t\times\text{max}(|\tilde{w}|)" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mtext>max</mtext></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>w</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta_{l}=t\times\text{max}(|\tilde{w}|)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(9)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">and 2) maintain a constant sparsity <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math> for all layers throughout training. By adjusting the hyper-parameter <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math> we are able to obtain ternary weight networks with various sparsities. We use the first method and set <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> to 0.05 in experiments on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet dataset and use the second one to explore a wider range of sparsities in section 5.1.1.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F2" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="1612.01064v3/weights.svg" id="S4.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:494/208;" width="494" height="208"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 2: </span>Ternary weights value (above) and distribution (below) with iterations for different layers of ResNet-20 on CIFAR-10.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We perform our experiments on CIFAR-10 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Krizhevsky &amp; Hinton, 2009</a>)</cite> and ImageNet <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Russakovsky et al., 2015</a>)</cite>.
Our network is implemented on both TensorFlow <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Abadi &amp; et. al o, 2015</a>)</cite> and Caffe <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jia et al., 2014</a>)</cite> frameworks.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>CIFAR-10</h3>

</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Experiments</h2>

<figure id="S5.F3" class="ltx_figure"><img src="1612.01064v3/accuracy.png" id="S5.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:494/228;" width="494" height="228" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 3: </span>ResNet-20 on CIFAR-10 with different weight precision.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">CIFAR-10 is an image classification benchmark containing images of size 32<math id="S5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math>32RGB pixels in a training set of 50000 and a test set of 10000. ResNet <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">He et al., 2015</a>)</cite> structure is used for our experiments.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We use parameters pre-trained from a full precision ResNet to initialize our model. Learning rate is set to 0.1 at beginning and scaled by 0.1 at epoch 80, 120 and 300. A L2-normalized weight decay of 0.0002 is used as regularizer. Most of our models converge after 160 epochs. We take a moving average on errors of all epochs to filter off fluctuations when reporting error rate.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We compare our model with the full-precision model and a binary-weight model. We train a a full precision ResNet <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">He et al., 2016</a>)</cite> on CIFAR-10 as the baseline (blue line in Figure <a href="#S5.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Trained Ternary Quantization" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>). We fine-tune the trained baseline network as a 1-32-32 DoReFa-Net where weights are 1 bit and both activations and gradients are 32 bits giving a significant loss of accuracy (green line) . Finally, we fine-tuning the baseline with trained ternary weights (red line). Our model has substantial accuracy improvement over the binary weight model, and our loss of accuracy over the full precision model is small. We also compare our model to Tenary Weight Network (TWN) on ResNet-20. Result shows our model improves the accuracy by <math id="S5.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim 0.25\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mn>0.25</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim 0.25\%</annotation></semantics></math> on CIFAR-10.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p4.1" class="ltx_p">We expand our experiments to ternarize ResNet with 32, 44 and 56 layers. All ternary models are fine-tuned from full precision models. Our results show that we improve the accuracy of ResNet-32, ResNet-44 and ResNet-56 by 0.04%, 0.16% and 0.36% . The deeper the model, the larger the improvement. We conjecture that this is due to ternary weights providing the right model capacity and preventing overfitting for deeper networks.</p>
</div>

<td id="S5.T1.2.5.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_b"><span id="S5.T1.2.5.4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">0.36</span></td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 1: </span>Error rates of full-precision and ternary ResNets on Cifar-10</figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="S5.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.1 </span>ImageNet</h3>

<div id="S5.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We further train and evaluate our model on ILSVRC12(<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Russakovsky et al. (2015)</a></cite>). ILSVRC12 is a 1000-category dataset with over 1.2 million images in training set and 50 thousand images in validation set. Images from ILSVRC12 also have various resolutions. We used a variant of AlexNet(<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Krizhevsky et al. (2012)</a></cite>) structure by removing dropout layers and add batch normalization<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ioffe &amp; Szegedy, 2015</a>)</cite> for all models in our experiments. The same variant is also used in experiments described in the paper of DoReFa-Net.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Our ternary model of AlexNet uses full precision weights for the first convolution layer and the last fully-connected layer. Other layer parameters are all quantized to ternary values. We train our model on ImageNet from scratch using an Adam optimizer (<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kingma &amp; Ba (2014)</a></cite>). Minibatch size is set to 128. Learning rate starts at <math id="S5.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10^{-4}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10^{-4}</annotation></semantics></math> and is scaled by 0.2 at epoch 56 and 64. A L2-normalized weight decay of <math id="S5.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="5\times 10^{-6}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>5</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5\times 10^{-6}</annotation></semantics></math> is used as a regularizer. Images are first resized to <math id="S5.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="256\times 256" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>256</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>256</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">256\times 256</annotation></semantics></math> then randomly cropped to <math id="S5.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="224\times 224" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>224</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>224</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">224\times 224</annotation></semantics></math> before input. We report both top 1 and top 5 error rate on validation set.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We compare our model to a full precision baseline, 1-32-32 DoReFa-Net and TWN. After around 64 epochs, validation error of our model dropped significantly compared to other low-bit networks as well as the full precision baseline. Finally our model reaches top 1 error rate of 42.5%, while DoReFa-Net gets 46.1% and TWN gets 45.5%. Furthermore, our model still outperforms full precision AlexNet (the batch normalization version, 44.1% according to paper of DoReFa-Net) by 1.6%, and is even better than the best AlexNet results reported (42.8%<span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
              
              
              
            https://github.com/BVLC/caffe/wiki/Models-accuracy-on-ImageNet-2012-val</span></span></span>). The complete results are listed in Table <a href="#S5.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 5.1 ImageNet ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Trained Ternary Quantization" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>.</p>
</div>

</figure>
<div id="S5.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">We draw the process of training in Figure <a href="#S5.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 5.1 ImageNet ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Trained Ternary Quantization" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, the baseline results of AlexNet are marked with dashed lines. Our ternary model effectively reduces the gap between training and validation performance, which appears to be quite great for DoReFa-Net and TWN. This indicates that adopting trainable <math id="S5.SS1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W^{p}_{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>W</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>p</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W^{p}_{l}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S5.SS1.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W^{n}_{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>W</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>n</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W^{n}_{l}</annotation></semantics></math> helps prevent models from overfitting to the training set.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">We also report the results of our methods on ResNet-18B in Table <a href="#S5.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 5.1 ImageNet ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Trained Ternary Quantization" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>. The full-precision error rates are obtained from Facebook’s implementation. Here we cite Binarized Weight Network(BWN)<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rastegari et al. (2016)</a></cite> results with all layers quantized and TWN finetuned based on a full precision network, while we train our TTQ model from scratch. Compared with BWN and TWN, our method obtains a substantial improvement.</p>
</div>

<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Discussion</h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section we analyze performance of our model with regard to weight compression and inference speeding up. These two goals are achieved through reducing bit precision and introducing sparsity. We also visualize convolution kernels in quantized convolution layers to find that basic patterns of edge/corner detectors are also well learned from scratch even precision is low.</p>
</div>
<section id="S6.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">6.1 </span>Spatial and energy efficiency</h3>

<div id="S6.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We save storage for models by <math id="S6.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="16\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>16</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">16\times</annotation></semantics></math> by using ternary weights. Although switching from a binary-weight network to a ternary-weight network increases bits per weight, it brings sparsity to the weights, which gives potential to skip the computation on zero weights and achieve higher energy efficiency.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S6.F5" class="ltx_figure"><img src="1612.01064v3/sparsity.png" id="S6.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:466/203;" width="466" height="203" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 5: </span>Accuracy v.s. Sparsity on ResNet-20</figcaption>
</figure>

<td id="S6.T4.2.9.7" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_r ltx_border_t">2 bit</td></tr>
<tr id="S6.T4.2.10" class="ltx_tr">

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 4: </span>Alexnet layer-wise sparsity</figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="S6.SS1.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">6.1.1 </span>Trade-off between sparsity and accuracy</h4>

<div id="S6.SS1.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS1.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S6.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ 6.1 Spatial and energy efficiency ‣ 6 Discussion ‣ Trained Ternary Quantization" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> shows the relationship between sparsity and accuracy. As the sparsity of weights grows from 0 (a pure binary-weight network) to 0.5 (a ternary network with 50% zeros), both the training and validation error decrease. Increasing sparsity beyond 50% reduces the model capacity too far, increasing error. Minimum error occurs with sparsity between 30% and 50%.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS1.SSS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS1.SSS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We introduce only one hyper-parameter to reduce search space. This hyper-parameter can be either sparsity, or the threshold <math id="S6.SS1.SSS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> w.r.t the max value in Equation 6.
We find that using threshold produces better results. This is because fixing the threshold allows the sparsity of each layer to vary (Figure reffig:weights).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS1.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">6.1.2 </span>Sparsity and efficiency of AlexNet</h4>

<div id="S6.SS1.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS1.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We further analyze parameters from our AlexNet model. We calculate layer-wise density (complement of sparsity) as shown in Table <a href="#S6.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ 6.1 Spatial and energy efficiency ‣ 6 Discussion ‣ Trained Ternary Quantization" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>. Despite we use different <math id="S6.SS1.SSS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W^{p}_{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>W</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>p</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W^{p}_{l}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S6.SS1.SSS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W^{n}_{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>W</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>n</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W^{n}_{l}</annotation></semantics></math> for each layer, ternary weights can be pre-computed when fetched from memory, thus multiplications during convolution and inner product process are still saved. Compared to Deep Compression, we accelerate inference speed using ternary values and more importantly, we reduce energy consumption of inference by saving memory references and multiplications, while achieving higher accuracy.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS1.SSS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS1.SSS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We notice that without all quantized layers sharing the same <math id="S6.SS1.SSS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> for Equation <a href="#S4.E9" title="In 4.2 Quantization Heuristic ‣ 4 Method ‣ Trained Ternary Quantization" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a>, our model achieves considerable sparsity in convolution layers where the majority of computations takes place. Therefore we are able to squeeze forward time to less than 30% of full precision networks.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS1.SSS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS1.SSS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">As for spatial compression, by substituting 32-bit weights with 2-bit ternary weights, our model is approximately <math id="S6.SS1.SSS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="16\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>16</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">16\times</annotation></semantics></math> smaller than original 32-bit AlexNet.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">6.2 </span>Kernel Visualization</h3>

<div id="S6.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We visualize quantized convolution kernels in Figure <a href="#S6.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ 6.2 Kernel Visualization ‣ 6 Discussion ‣ Trained Ternary Quantization" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>. The left matrix is kernels from the second convolution layer (<math id="S6.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="5\times 5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>5</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5\times 5</annotation></semantics></math>) and the right one is from the third (<math id="S6.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="3\times 3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3\times 3</annotation></semantics></math>). We pick first 10 input channels and first 10 output channels to display for each layer. Grey, black and white color represent zero, negative and positive weights respectively.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We observe similar filter patterns as full precision AlexNet. Edge and corner detectors of various directions can be found among listed kernels. While these patterns are important for convolution neural networks, the precision of each weight is not. Ternary value filters are capable enough extracting key features after a full precision first convolution layer while saving unnecessary storage.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Furthermore, we find that there are a number of empty filters (all zeros) or filters with single non-zero value in convolution layers. More aggressive pruning can be applied to prune away these redundant kernels to further compress and speed up our model.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S6.F6" class="ltx_figure"><img src="1612.01064v3/kernels.png" id="S6.F6.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:548/267;" width="548" height="267" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 6: </span>Visualization of kernels from Ternary AlexNet trained from Imagenet.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S7" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">7 </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S7.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We introduce a novel neural network quantization method that compresses network weights to ternary values. We introduce two trained scaling coefficients <math id="S7.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W^{l}_{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>W</mi><mi>p</mi><mi>l</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W^{l}_{p}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S7.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W^{l}_{n}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>W</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>l</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W^{l}_{n}</annotation></semantics></math> for each layer and train these coefficients using back-propagation. During training, the gradients are back-propagated both to the latent full-resolution weights and to the scaling coefficients. We use layer-wise thresholds that are proportional to the maximum absolute values to quantize the weights. When deploying the ternary network, only the ternary weights and scaling coefficients are needed, which reducing parameter size by at least <math id="S7.p1.m3" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="16\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>16</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">16\times</annotation></semantics></math>. Experiments show that our model reaches or even surpasses the accuracy of full precision models on both CIFAR-10 and ImageNet dataset. On ImageNet we exceed the accuracy of prior ternary networks (TWN) by 3%.</p>
</div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
</section>

    target="_blank" rel="nofollow">view the build logs</a>
    for errors. Generated by
    <a href="https://math.nist.gov/~BMiller/LaTeXML/" target="_blank" class="ltx_ref ltx_LaTeXML_logo">
      <span style="letter-spacing: -0.2em; margin-right: 0.1em;">
        L
        <span style="font-size: 70%; position: relative; bottom: 2.2pt;">A</span>
        T
        <span style="position: relative; bottom: -0.4ex;">E</span>
      </span>
      <span class="ltx_font_smallcaps">xml</span>
      <img alt="[LOGO]"
        src="data:image/png;base64,">
    </a>.
  </div>
  <div class="keyboard-glossary">
    <h2>Instructions for reporting errors</h2>
    <p>We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile
      support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the
      methods listed below:</p>
    <ul>
      <li>Click the "Report Issue" <span class="mobile-only">(<svg role="presentation"
            style="display: inline-block; vertical-align: middle; fill: var(--text-color);" aria-hidden="true"
            height="1em" viewBox="0 0 640 640">
            <path
              d="M224 160C224 107 267 64 320 64C373 64 416 107 416 160L416 163.6C416 179.3 403.3 192 387.6 192L252.5 192C236.8 192 224.1 179.3 224.1 163.6L224.1 160zM569.6 172.8C580.2 186.9 577.3 207 563.2 217.6L465.4 290.9C470.7 299.8 474.7 309.6 477.2 320L576 320C593.7 320 608 334.3 608 352C608 369.7 593.7 384 576 384L480 384L480 416C480 418.6 479.9 421.3 479.8 423.9L563.2 486.4C577.3 497 580.2 517.1 569.6 531.2C559 545.3 538.9 548.2 524.8 537.6L461.7 490.3C438.5 534.5 395.2 566.5 344 574.2L344 344C344 330.7 333.3 320 320 320C306.7 320 296 330.7 296 344L296 574.2C244.8 566.5 201.5 534.5 178.3 490.3L115.2 537.6C101.1 548.2 81 545.3 70.4 531.2C59.8 517.1 62.7 497 76.8 486.4L160.2 423.9C160.1 421.3 160 418.7 160 416L160 384L64 384C46.3 384 32 369.7 32 352C32 334.3 46.3 320 64 320L162.8 320C165.3 309.6 169.3 299.8 174.6 290.9L76.8 217.6C62.7 207 59.8 186.9 70.4 172.8C81 158.7 101.1 155.8 115.2 166.4L224 248C236.3 242.9 249.8 240 264 240L376 240C390.2 240 403.7 242.8 416 248L524.8 166.4C538.9 155.8 559 158.7 569.6 172.8z" />
          </svg>)</span> button, located in the page header.</li>
    </ul>
    <p><strong>Tip:</strong> You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.</p>
    <p>Our team has already identified <a class="ltx_ref" href="https://github.com/arXiv/html_feedback/issues"
        target="_blank">the following issues</a>. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we
      may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability
      should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for
      all.</p>
    <p>Have a free development cycle? Help support accessibility at arXiv! Our collaborators at LaTeXML maintain a <a
        class="ltx_ref" href="https://github.com/brucemiller/LaTeXML/wiki/Porting-LaTeX-packages-for-LaTeXML"
        target="_blank">list of packages that need conversion</a>, and welcome <a class="ltx_ref"
        href="https://github.com/brucemiller/LaTeXML/issues" target="_blank">developer contributions</a>.</p>
  </div>
